# Library API reference

<!-- Generated by tools/api_reference.py from the code; do not edit by hand. -->

Everything here is what library code (generators, PartScripts, loss and
friction functions) may use. It reaches library code through its context:
`context["hvac_api"]` is the geometry API, `context["loss_api"]` the loss
API. Library code never imports FreeCAD, Part or internal HVAC modules; how
to write a library, and what library code may do with the shapes the API
returns, is in [the library guide](library-guide.md).

A change to any public name or context key raises the matching
`API_VERSION`; a library declares the versions it was written for in its
`library.json` (`"requires_api"`) and is refused by any other (see
`CHANGELOG.md`, "Compatibility policy").

## Geometry API: `HVACLibraryAPI` (version 4)

### Constants

#### `API_VERSION`

Value: `4`.

#### `EPS`

Length tolerance, mm: `1e-09`.

#### `PUBLIC`

The set of public names (this page).

#### `STANDARD_FITTINGS`

The fitting names `build_fitting` and `measure_fitting` accept: `ahu`, `cross_tee_straight`, `double_wye_mitered`, `double_wye_radius`, `duct_closure`, `elbow`, `elbow_mitered`, `inline_damper`, `inline_obstruction`, `inline_vav`, `plenum`, `star_branch`, `star_cross`, `star_multiport`, `star_wye`, `tap_saddle`, `tap_shoe`, `tap_straight`, `tee_lateral`, `tee_lateral_mitered`, `tee_lateral_radius`, `tee_mitered_shoe`, `tee_radius_center`, `tee_radius_edge`, `tee_straight`, `terminal_bellmouth`, `terminal_body`, `terminal_cone`, `terminal_diffusing`, `terminal_frame`, `terminal_hood`, `terminal_plain`, `terminal_round`, `terminal_slot`, `terminal_square`, `through`, `transition`, `transition_mitered`, `transition_radiussed`, `wye_mitered`, `wye_radius`.

### Ports, vectors and lines

#### `angle_between(u1, u2)`

Return the smaller angle between two vectors in radians.

#### `arc_center_from_points_tangents_radius(p0, p1, u0, u1, radius)`

Compute the center of a circular arc joining p0 -> p1 with given radius,
using tangent directions u0 at p0 and u1 at p1.

Parameters
----------
p0, p1 : FreeCAD.Vector
    Arc end points.
u0, u1 : FreeCAD.Vector
    Tangent directions at p0 and p1.
radius : float
    Arc radius.

Returns
-------
FreeCAD.Vector
    Arc center.

Notes
-----
- The bend plane is derived from u0 x u1.
- The chosen center is the one whose radius vectors are most
  perpendicular to the supplied tangents.

#### `average_point(points)`

Return the arithmetic mean of points, or the origin for an empty input.

#### `build_trim_rec_from_context_uniform(context, length_value)`

Same as build_trim_rec_from_port_lengths, but trims every connected port by the same length_value.

#### `build_trim_rec_from_port_lengths(port_lengths)`

Build the connection_lengths a generator returns from a list of
(port, trim_length) pairs -- how far each connected segment is
trimmed back from its own endpoint to make room for this fitting.
Ports with no real edge_key/segment_end (e.g. a synthetic port) are
silently skipped.

#### `center_from_context(context)`

The junction's center point, or (if not given) the average of its connected ports' positions.

#### `closest_points_on_lines(p0, d0, p1, d1)`

Return closest points c0 on L0 and c1 on L1 for:

    L0(t) = p0 + t d0
    L1(s) = p1 + s d1

Returns (None, None) for nearly parallel lines.

#### `collinear_port_index_pairs(context)`

Index pairs (into ``connected_ports(context)``) the network
classifier already found collinear (~180 deg apart -- see
``NetworkParser._collinear_pairs``), read straight off the
junction's own ``context["analysis"]["collinear_pairs"]`` payload
(``NetworkParser.JunctionAnalysis``, propagated via
``Component._parentAnalysis``/``AnalysisJson``).

A "which two of this node's ports form the straight run" generator
(a radiused/mitered tee's trunk, a tap's main run, ...) should use
this rather than re-deriving collinearity itself, so it agrees
exactly with the classifier's own family_key decision (same
tolerance, same data) instead of risking a second, possibly
divergent judgment call. Empty if no analysis payload is present
(e.g. a synthetic/unit-test context) -- callers need their own
geometric fallback for that case.

#### `connected_ports(context)`

Return a copy of the context's connected-port list.

#### `copy_port(port, position=None, direction=None, profile_x_axis=None, edge_key=None, segment_end=None)`

Copy a port dict, optionally overriding position/direction/
profile_x_axis/edge_key/segment_end (everything else unchanged).

edge_key/segment_end are useful when synthesizing a port that
doesn't correspond to the original port's own connection any more
(e.g. an internal seam between two chained junction components).

#### `grow_port_section(port, delta)`

Copy of `port` with its cross-section grown by `delta` (uniformly,
on every side) -- position/direction/profile are unchanged, only
section_params grows. Shared helper for building an insulation (or
any other wrap-around) shape's own outer profile from a casing
port's profile, without duplicating this per fitting generator.
Used for a flange collar (it sits on the outside of the wall) and
for any other shape wrapped around a port's own section.

#### `is_zero(v, eps=None)`

Return whether *v* is no longer than the requested tolerance.

#### `port_area(port)`

Cross-section area (m^2) of a port, from its profile/section_params (in mm).

#### `port_diameter(port)`

Return a circular port's diameter in millimetres, defaulting to zero.

#### `port_direction(port)`

Return a port's outward direction as a unit vector.

#### `port_height(port)`

Return a rectangular or oval port's height in millimetres.

#### `port_param(context, name, port, default=None)`

A property value for one port.

Works for a per-port property (a type-def property marked
`"per_port": true`, resolved to one value per connected port) and
for an ordinary property (one value shared by every port), so a
generator need not know which of the two a type declares. `default`
is returned when the property is missing or not set for that port.

#### `port_position(port)`

Return a port's position as a FreeCAD vector.

#### `port_profile(port)`

Return the normalized profile name stored on a port.

#### `port_profile_x_axis(port)`

Return a port's profile x-axis, or ``None`` when it is unavailable.

#### `port_roles(context)`

The connected ports of the current node, by role name. The roles
depend only on how many ports there are and how they are arranged:

- 1 port:  neck
- 2 ports: inlet, outlet (by flow direction; port order if unknown)
- 3 ports with a straight run (a tee, a lateral): run_a, run_b, branch
- 3 ports with no straight run (a wye): main, branch_a, branch_b
- 4 ports with a straight run (a cross, a double wye):
  run_a, run_b, branch_a, branch_b
- anything else, including 5 or more ports: port_1 .. port_n

"Straight run" is the classifier's own collinear pair, so this
never disagrees with the family the node was given. For port_1..n
the order is geometric (by outward direction), so it does not
depend on the order the ports happen to be listed in.

#### `port_section_params(port)`

Return a copy of a port's section-parameter mapping.

#### `port_width(port)`

Return a rectangular or oval port's width in millimetres.

#### `rotate_vector(v, axis, angle)`

Rotate vector *v* by *angle* radians around a unit *axis* (Rodrigues' formula).

#### `run_branch_ports(context)`

Return ``(run_a, run_b, branch)`` for a degree-three tee/tap.

The run pair comes from the network classifier's collinear-pair
analysis. Port roles are not guessed again from raw geometry here.

#### `unit(v, eps=None)`

Return a normalized copy of *v*, rejecting a zero-length vector.

#### `vec(v)`

Return *v* as a FreeCAD vector.

#### `xyz(v)`

Return a vector-like value as an ``(x, y, z)`` tuple.

### Section wires and frames

#### `make_circular_wire(center, normal, diameter)`

A circular section wire, centered on `center`, lying in the plane perpendicular to `normal`.

#### `make_circular_wire_split_at(center, normal, diameter, directions)`

A circle drawn as one arc per entry of `directions`, with a corner
where each direction (from the centre, projected onto the circle's
plane) crosses it.

Use it where a sweep or loft goes from a section with corners (one
half of a split profile) to a circle: a circle with the same number
of corners, placed to match, keeps the solid from twisting.

#### `make_profile_frame(direction, preferred_x=None, origin=None)`

Build a right-handed section frame whose z-axis follows *direction*.

#### `make_rectangular_wire(center, x_axis, y_axis, width, height)`

A rectangular section wire, centered on `center` and aligned to x_axis/y_axis.

#### `make_split_circular_wire(center, x_axis, y_axis, diameter, width, height)`

A circle drawn as four arcs, split where the lines from its centre to
the corners of a width x height rectangle (on the same axes) cross it.

A plain circle is one edge with its seam wherever OCC puts it, so a
loft from it to a rectangle twists. This one has a corner for each
corner of the rectangle, in the same order as make_rectangular_wire,
so the two loft edge for edge.

### Profiles and solids

#### `extrude(profile, vector, *, solid=False)`

Extrude a profile or wire along a nonzero vector.

With ``solid=True`` the wire is first converted to a face, producing a
solid extrusion. Otherwise the wire itself is extruded into a shell.

#### `loft(profiles, *, solid=False, ruled=True, closed=False)`

Loft through at least two profiles and return the resulting shape.

#### `make_face(profile)`

A flat face filling a closed profile or planar wire (its outline only, no holes).

#### `make_profile(profile_type, params, frame=None, *, center=None, direction=None, profile_x_axis=None)`

Build a closed section wire in a local placement frame.

``profile_type`` accepts rectangular, circular, oval, rounded-
rectangle, and polygon aliases. ``frame`` may be a mapping with
origin/normal/x-axis entries or a three-item sequence; explicit frame
keyword arguments fill any values omitted by a mapping.

Returns an :class:`HVACProfile`. Invalid or collapsed dimensions raise
``ValueError``.

#### `offset_profile(profile, distance)`

Return a new profile offset uniformly in its local section plane.

Positive distances grow the clear-air boundary and negative distances
shrink it. The input must be an ``HVACProfile`` returned by this API.

#### `offset_wire(wire, distance)`

Grow (positive distance) or shrink (negative) any closed planar wire
in its own plane, keeping sharp corners sharp.

Use `offset_profile()` for a normal section profile -- it rebuilds
the section exactly from its own dimensions. This is for a wire that
is no longer a plain section, e.g. one half of a split profile or a
section cut off a mitred body.

#### `profile_from_port(port, offset=0.0)`

Build an ``HVACProfile`` from a library port.

A positive ``offset`` grows the port section uniformly before the
profile is built; a negative value shrinks it.

#### `profile_projection_bounds(profile, direction)`

Return the minimum and maximum projection of a profile along direction.

#### `revolve(profile, axis, angle=360.0, *, solid=False)`

Revolve a profile around ``(origin, direction)`` by degrees.

``axis`` may also be a mapping with ``origin`` and ``direction`` (or
``axis``) entries. ``solid=True`` revolves the profile's filled face.

#### `rotate(shape, origin, axis, degrees)`

A copy of ``shape`` turned by ``degrees`` about the line through ``origin`` along ``axis``.

#### `sample_path(path, spacing)`

Points along a path edge (or a wire of edges), ``spacing`` apart, as
``[(point, unit tangent), ...]``. The stations are centred: whatever
length is left over is split evenly between both ends, so a row of
ribs or hangers sits symmetrically. Fewer than one ``spacing`` of
path gives an empty list.

#### `split_profile_face_by_extent(profile, split_direction, positive_ratio)`

Split a profile at a linear ratio of its projected extent.

The requested direction snaps to the nearest local horizontal or
vertical axis. The positive face points with that oriented axis.

#### `stretch_profile_one_sided(profile, direction, extension)`

Stretch a profile along direction while keeping its heel side fixed.

The profile's minimum projection along direction is treated as the heel.
The opposite side is extended by ``extension``. No assumption is made
about profile type or geometry.

#### `sweep(profiles, path, *, solid=False, frenet=False, transition=0)`

Sweep one or more section profiles along a path wire.

``frenet`` and ``transition`` are forwarded to OCC's pipe-shell
builder. A failed, null, or non-solid result (when ``solid=True``)
raises ``RuntimeError`` with a stable library-facing message.

#### `translate(shape, vector)`

A copy of ``shape`` moved by ``vector``.

### Booleans and shape tools

#### `clip_plane(shape, plane, side='positive')`

Keep one half of ``shape`` relative to an infinite plane.

``plane`` is ``(origin, normal)`` or a mapping. ``side`` accepts
positive/front/normal or negative/back/opposite aliases.

#### `common(*shapes, refine=False)`

Intersect nested shape arguments, optionally removing splitters.

#### `compound(shapes)`

Create a compound from nested non-null shape sequences.

#### `cut(shape, *tools, refine=False)`

Subtract each non-null tool from ``shape`` in argument order.

#### `fuse(*shapes, refine=False)`

Fuse nested shape arguments, optionally removing splitters.

#### `make_line(start, end)`

Create a line edge between two distinct points.

#### `make_sphere(center, diameter)`

Create a sphere from its center and positive diameter.

#### `refine(shape)`

Remove boolean splitters when OCC can do so safely.

Merging faces sometimes turns a valid shape into an invalid one
(seen on fused swept bodies, where a later cut then gives a wrong
result). In that case the original, unrefined shape is returned.

#### `reverse(shape)`

Return a copy with reversed topology orientation.

#### `section_face(shape, plane)`

Return the exact planar cross-section where ``shape`` meets a plane.

``plane`` is ``(origin, normal)`` or a mapping, same as
``clip_plane``. This is the ready-made face a neighbouring piece
should be built against after ``clip_plane`` trims a shape back to
a cut line (e.g. a mitre plane) -- reading the real cut face back
off the trimmed shape avoids any mismatch against an independently
built, idealised profile that might not land exactly on the plane.

Reads the face directly off ``shape.Faces`` rather than
intersecting with a fresh plane face: a plane coincident with (part
of) the shape's own boundary -- exactly the case right after
``clip_plane`` cut it there -- is a tangential/degenerate boolean
for OCC, which is unreliable (it can silently return empty). The
cut face is already a real face of ``shape``; this just finds it.

#### `trim(shape, boundary, keep='inside')`

Trim ``shape`` with a plane or another Part shape.

Shape boundaries support intersection (``inside``) and difference
(``outside``). Plane mappings use their own optional ``side`` value
and default to the positive half-space.

#### `validate(shape, *, raise_on_error=False, require_solid=False)`

Return a stable diagnostic dictionary for a Part shape.

Set ``require_solid`` to treat shapes without solids as invalid and
``raise_on_error`` to raise ``ValueError`` instead of only reporting
accumulated messages.

### Paths, fittings and layers

#### `build_envelopes(envelope_builder, construction_layers, params)`

Build the nested outer envelopes of a multilayer wall, from the
clear-air boundary outward.

`envelope_builder(offset)` builds the fitting's *whole* outer
boundary shape uniformly offset outward by `offset` from the
clear-air boundary (an offset of 0 is the air envelope itself) --
a generator builds this closure once, from its own profiles/path/
mitre-plane logic (typically via `profile_from_port(..., offset)`),
and this method is the only thing that ever calls it, so every
layer reuses exactly the same axes/stations/trim planes.

`construction_layers` is the type-def's own declared construction
layers, in order (`context["construction_layers"]`, a list of
library/construction.py's ConstructionLayerDef). Each layer's
thickness is read from `params[layer.thickness_property]`; a layer
with no `thickness_property` contributes zero thickness (e.g. a
purely descriptive layer with no wall thickness of its own).

Returns `[air, envelope_1, envelope_2, ..., envelope_N]` -- one
more shape than there are layers. A zero-thickness layer's
envelope is the same object as the envelope before it (no
redundant rebuild), which is how `envelopes_to_layers` recognizes
it below.

#### `build_fitting(name, context)`

Build one of the standard fittings (see STANDARD_FITTINGS) for the
given geometry context: its hollow, layered shape plus its trims,
as the usual `{"layers": ..., "connection_lengths": ...}` dict. The
wall build-up comes from the context's construction layers and their
thickness properties; flanges are the type's construction feature,
not part of this result.

#### `build_layered_fitting(context, envelope_builder, connection_lengths, port_roles=None)`

Finish a custom fitting the same way the standard ones are finished.

`envelope_builder(offset)` returns the fitting's outer boundary as a
solid, grown outward by `offset` from the air space. This cuts every
declared construction layer out of it, adds flanges at the fitting
ends when the type declares FlangeThickness/FlangeHeight, and
returns the result dict with `connection_lengths` attached.
`port_roles` optionally maps edge_key -> role name (e.g. "Branch")
for per-port ShowFlange<Role> switches.

#### `build_layered_geometry(envelope_builder, construction_layers, params)`

Convenience wrapper: `build_envelopes()` + `envelopes_to_layers()`,
packaged as the `{"layers": {id: {"shape": ...}}}` dict a geometry
backend returns (see library/geometry_result.py's `normalize()`).

This is the one call most multilayer fitting generators need: build
`envelope_builder(offset)` once from the fitting's own geometry
context, then hand it here together with `context["construction_layers"]`
and the resolved `params` -- no per-fitting casing/insulation-specific
layer helpers required.

#### `envelopes_to_layers(envelopes)`

Cut `HVACLibraryAPI.build_envelopes()`'s nested envelopes into each
layer's own physical solid: Layer 1 = Envelope 1 - Air,
Layer 2 = Envelope 2 - Envelope 1, ..., innermost layer first.

A layer whose envelope is the same object as the one before it (a
zero-thickness layer, see `build_envelopes`) is reported as `None`
without running a boolean at all.

#### `make_elbow_path(port0, port1, radius)`

Create the tangent arc and trimmed ports for a two-port elbow.

Returns a dict containing ``path``, tangent ``ports``, and
``trim_lengths``. Callers can build matching offset profiles at those
ports and pass them to :meth:`sweep`.

#### `make_flange(port, inward_direction, thickness, height)`

Build a flat annular flange collar around any supported port profile.

#### `make_radiussed_path(port0, port1, length, radius)`

Create a radiussed offset path between two parallel ports.

The path consists of:

    straight -> circular arc -> diagonal -> circular arc -> straight

The fitting has an axial length of ``length``.  The theoretical sharp
turn points are located at 1/4 of the fitting length from each generated
port.  ``radius`` specifies the radius of both circular bends.

The input port directions are outward and must therefore be opposite.

Returns a dict containing ``path``, trimmed ``ports``,
``trim_lengths``, and ``turn_points``.

#### `measure_fitting(name, context)`

The trim records of a standard fitting, without building any shape.

#### `offset_transition_axis(port0, port1, length)`

Shared axis geometry for a two-port lateral-offset transition.

Both ports face outward in opposite, parallel directions but sit on
offset (non-coincident) axes -- the generic "through.offset" case.
This works out the end points and theoretical sharp turn points
that every offset-transition builder needs, so the radiussed
(arc-filleted) and mitered (flat-cut) builders agree on exactly the
same axis and only differ in how the corner itself is finished.

Step 1: find the travel direction and the two generated end points,
``length`` apart, that preserve the ports' lateral (transverse)
offset.
Step 2: find the theoretical sharp turn points -- a quarter of the
body length in from each end point -- and the direction/angle of
the diagonal segment connecting them.

Returns a dict with keys ``p0``/``p1``/``u0``/``u1`` (the original
port positions/outward directions), ``d`` (unit travel direction,
port0 -> port1), ``s0``/``s1`` (generated end points), ``corner0``/
``corner1`` (turn points), ``diagonal`` (unit corner0 -> corner1
direction), and ``turn_angle`` (radians, the deflection between the
end run and the diagonal -- zero for a plain straight run with no
lateral offset).

#### `resolve_library_file(context, relative_path)`

Resolve a path relative to the current type-def's own library folder (e.g. a data file it ships with).

#### `shape_from_fcstd(fcstd_path, context, params=None, result_object='Result', port_names=None, tol_mm=0.5, tol_deg=0.5)`

Build a shape from an FCStd template file (a parametric sketch-driven model) -- see template_shapes.py.

#### `single_layer(context, shape, **extra)`

The `{"layers": ...}` result for a fitting built as one solid (a
marker, a cap, a fitting with no wall): the shape goes on the type's
first declared construction layer, or on a layer named "shape" when
it declares none. Any `extra` keys (connection_lengths, ...) are
added to the result. The `{"shape": ...}` result form was removed:
every backend returns layers.

## Loss API: `HVACLossAPI` (version 1)

### Constants

#### `API_VERSION`

Value: `1`.

#### `APPROXIMATION`

A LossStatus constant.

#### `CUSTOM`

A LossStatus constant.

#### `EXACT`

A LossStatus constant.

#### `FALLBACK`

A LossStatus constant.

#### `PUBLIC`

The set of public names (this page).

#### `UNSUPPORTED`

A LossStatus constant.

### Loss functions

#### `branch_loss(context)`

Converging (merging) or diverging (splitting) tee/wye fitting loss.
Expects exactly 3 connected_ports: one "common"/trunk port (the sole
inlet if diverging, the sole outlet if converging) and two "secondary"
ports (branch + straight-through), identified by which secondary
port's direction is closest to anti-parallel with the common port's
direction (the straight-through continuation of the duct run).

properties["BranchStyle"] picks how the branch is joined (see
_tee_zetas for the table each reads): "straight" (default),
"conical", "45_entry", "damper", "45_entry_damper", "extractor".

Returns two LossPaths (branch, straight), each referenced to that
leg's own velocity: EXACT when every lookup was inside a printed
table made for this fitting, APPROXIMATION (with the reason) when
not, UNSUPPORTED for an ambiguous/degenerate flow pattern or
invalid geometry.

#### `branch_loss_bullhead(context)`

Bullhead tee/wye: the single common-flow port sits on the
geometric *branch* leg instead of the run (see NetworkParser's
qualifiers["common_leg"] == "branch" -- library JSON loss.variants
route here for exactly that case, distinct from the ordinary
common_leg == "run" case branch_loss() above already handles
correctly). Expects exactly 3 connected_ports.

This is a generic APPROXIMATION (see _no_straight_leg_branch_zetas),
not a validated SMACNA table entry for a bullhead arrangement --
never presented to a caller as an EXACT table result.

Returns one LossPath per run leg, each already referenced to that
leg's own velocity, or UNSUPPORTED for an ambiguous/degenerate flow
pattern or invalid geometry.

#### `damper_loss(context)`

Loss of a damper at its current blade position (SMACNA Table 14-18
A to G). properties["DamperType"] picks the kind:

- "butterfly" (default): single thin blade. BladeAngle (0 = fully open).
- "butterfly_airfoil": single airfoil blade, rectangular. BladeAngle.
- "gate": sliding gate. GateOpening = open height over duct height (0 to 1).
- "parallel_blade" / "opposed_blade": multi-blade, rectangular.
  BladeAngle, BladeCount; the blades run along the duct width.

#### `elbow_loss(context)`

Loss of an elbow (SMACNA Table 14-10), for any turn angle.
properties["ElbowConstruction"] picks how the elbow is made:

- "smooth" (default): smooth radius. Round: 14-10 A. Rectangular:
  14-10 F, or 14-10 G when SplitterVanes is 1 to 3. Needs
  CenterlineRadius.
- "gored": made of straight pieces, NumberOfCuts + 1 of them. Round
  with 3 to 5 pieces: 14-10 B (needs CenterlineRadius). Two pieces
  is a plain mitered elbow (below). A gored rectangular elbow has
  no table; the smooth one is used and flagged.
- "mitered": one mitre joint. Round: 14-10 C. Rectangular: 14-10 D.
- "turning_vanes": rectangular, mitered, with turning vanes: 14-10 H
  for the VaneDesign given (see loss_tables.elbows.TURNING_VANES).

Expects exactly 2 connected ports (one inlet, one outlet). Returns
one LossPath referenced to the outlet's velocity: EXACT when the
point was inside the printed table, APPROXIMATION (with the reason)
when it was not, UNSUPPORTED when the fitting cannot be worked out.

#### `entry_loss(context)`

Loss of an entry: air entering the duct system from a room or from
outdoors (SMACNA Table 14-15). properties["EntryType"] picks the shape:

- "duct_in_wall" (default): plain duct end. WallThickness,
  ProjectionLength (how far it sticks out of the wall; 0 = flush).
- "bellmouth": rounded lip (round ducts). LipRadius, EndWall.
- "conical": cone or pyramid. ConeAngle (included), ConeLength, EndWall.
- "intake_hood": weather hood. HoodAngle (0 or 15), HoodHeight.
- "tapered_hood": capture hood. HoodAngle (included).
- "canopy_hood": kitchen canopy, one fixed coefficient.

ScreenFreeArea (0 to 1) adds a screen in the opening; OpeningAreaRatio
is that opening's area over the duct area (default 1).

#### `exit_loss(context)`

Loss of an exit: air leaving the duct system (SMACNA Table 14-16).
properties["ExitType"] picks the shape:

- "abrupt" (default): plain duct end, C = 1.
- "conical": round diffusing cone. ConeAngle (included), AreaRatio
  (exit area over duct area).
- "plane_diffuser": rectangular, one pair of sides diverging. ConeAngle, AreaRatio.
- "pyramidal_diffuser": rectangular, all sides diverging. ConeAngle, AreaRatio.
- "exhaust_hood": weather hood. HoodAngle (0 or 15), HoodHeight.

ScreenFreeArea (0 to 1) adds a screen in the exit opening.

#### `fan_connection_loss(context)`

The system-effect loss where a duct leaves a fan (an AHU's supply
connection), from properties["FanConnection"]:

- "Transition symmetric" / "... asymmetric top level" / "... top 10
  down" / "... top 10 up" / "... pyramidal": a transition from the
  fan outlet to the duct, SMACNA 14-11 F to J, at TransitionAngle
  and the area ratio duct / fan outlet.
- "Discharge into casing": the fan blows freely into the unit's own
  casing (a plenum) and the duct leaves that, 14-16 I, by FanWheel.

The fan outlet is the equipment port the end is connected to
(context "equipment_port"). The tables are
printed against the fan outlet's velocity; the result is referenced
to the duct's, K = C (A_duct / A_outlet)^2. Only for air leaving the
unit into the duct. "None" or no FanConnection: UNSUPPORTED (no fan
connection to cost), as is a duct that carries air into the unit.

#### `fixed_pressure_drop_loss(context)`

A device rated by a pressure drop instead of a coefficient (an air
terminal or a VAV box from a manufacturer's data sheet):
properties["PressureDrop"] in Pa, taken as given at the current flow.

The solver only works in coefficients, so the drop is turned into
the K that gives exactly that many Pa at the device's present
velocity: K = PressureDrop / (rho * V^2 / 2). Works for a 1-port
terminal and for a 2-port inline device (referenced to its outlet).
UNSUPPORTED when PressureDrop is not set.

#### `inline_device_loss(context)`

Generic inline device (damper, VAV box, ...) loss: a single
dimensionless coefficient K taken directly from
properties["LossCoefficient"], applied to the connecting duct's own
velocity pressure at the device's outlet. No neck-size conversion is
needed here (unlike terminal_component_loss) since these devices
carry the same duct through both ports rather than stepping down to
a separate neck size.

Expects exactly 2 connected_ports (one inlet, one outlet). Returns
one EXACT LossPath referenced to the outlet's own velocity
(matching the inline-chain convention analysis/pressure.py already
uses), or UNSUPPORTED if LossCoefficient isn't set (nothing to
compute) or the topology can't be resolved.

#### `manifold_loss(context)`

Cross (4-port) or multiport (5+ port) fitting loss, for the common
single-trunk case: exactly one port on one flow side (all inlet, or
all outlet) and the rest ("secondaries") on the other side.

No dedicated SMACNA/ASHRAE table exists for 4+ port fittings, so this
decomposes the junction into a sequence of pairwise branch (tee/wye)
calculations, reusing the exact same diverging_branch_zetas /
converging_branch_zetas tables as branch_loss: secondaries are
peeled off one at a time, least-straight (most branch-like) first,
straightest last -- mirroring how a real header/manifold is
typically laid out (larger/sharper takeoffs nearer the main
connection, the straightest path continuing furthest). Each pairwise
step is referenced against the PRIMARY port's own duct size and
direction (and, for the branch-angle lookup, the straightest
secondary's direction) as a stand-in for the intermediate duct
geometry this addon doesn't actually model between successive
virtual merges/splits -- an APPROXIMATION, not a literal per-leg
geometry readout. With exactly 2 secondaries this reduces to
exactly the same numbers as branch_loss's 3-port calculation.

Returns one LossPath per secondary port (each already referenced to
that leg's own velocity and to the primary port's own edge_key), or
UNSUPPORTED for a mixed multi-inlet/multi-outlet ("true cross") flow
pattern -- which has no single trunk to decompose against -- or on
any missing/invalid geometry.

#### `obstruction_loss(context)`

Loss of a smooth cylinder (a pipe, a rod) crossing the duct (SMACNA
Table 14-18 H). properties: ObstructionDiameter, and OffsetFromCentre
(distance of the cylinder axis from the duct centreline; 0 = centred).
In a rectangular duct the cylinder runs along the width and is
offset along the height.

Needs the air's kinematic viscosity and the duct velocity from the
solver context. With no flow the coefficient cannot be read (it
depends on the Reynolds number), so a zero loss is returned.

#### `offset_loss(context)`

Lateral-offset (jog) fitting loss: a same-size collinear pair whose
axes are transversely displaced -- the "through.offset" case (see
TOPOLOGY_CLASSIFICATION.md), as opposed to transition_loss's area
change. Expects exactly 2 connected_ports and the offset body's own
axial length in properties: "OffsetLength" (an offset type) or
"TransitionLength" (a transition-style type used for an offset).

Modelled as two corner deflections in series, each at the fitting's
own turn angle (HVACLibraryAPI.offset_transition_axis), using
SMACNA's generic-angle mitered-elbow tables (A7C/A7D) -- unlike the
90-deg-only smooth-radius tables (elbow_zeta_round/rect), these are
indexed by angle directly, which an offset's shallow corners need.
An "OffsetRadius"/"TransitionRadius" entry in properties (the
radiussed style) still borrows the mitered coefficient, since SMACNA has no
generic-angle smooth-radius table -- that case comes back as
APPROXIMATION rather than EXACT.

#### `plenum_loss(context)`

Loss of a plenum box, for any number of inlets and outlets.

The box is large enough for the air to come to rest in it, so each
inlet is an abrupt exit into the box (SMACNA Table 14-16, C = 1 on
the inlet velocity) and each outlet is a flush entry from it (Table
14-15 A, C = 0.5 on the outlet velocity). One LossPath per
inlet/outlet pair, referenced to the outlet:

    K = C_entry + C_exit * (V_inlet / V_outlet)^2

Always APPROXIMATION: the tables are for an opening in a large
space, which a real plenum only approaches.

#### `screen_loss(context)`

Loss of a screen or perforated plate across the duct (SMACNA Table
14-17). properties["FreeAreaRatio"] is the open fraction (0 to 1).
A perforated plate also sets PlateThickness and HoleDiameter; with
no HoleDiameter the fitting is treated as a wire screen.

#### `sum_losses(first, second)`

Two LossEvaluations of the same one-path fitting added together
(e.g. a unit's own coefficient plus its fan connection). An
UNSUPPORTED one is left out; the status is the weaker of the two
(EXACT only when both are), and warnings are joined.

#### `terminal_component_loss(context)`

Generic terminal air device (diffuser/grille/register) loss: a
dimensionless coefficient K (from properties["LossCoefficient"]),
referenced to velocity at the device's own neck
(properties["NeckSize"]) rather than the connecting duct's own
velocity -- the neck is often a different size than the duct feeding
it. Converted to a K_effective referenced to the connecting duct's
velocity (K_effective = K * (V_neck / V_duct)^2, since velocity
pressure ~ V^2 at constant density) so it composes with the solver's
existing K * velocity_pressure(duct) convention used for every other
fitting -- no special-casing needed downstream.

Expects exactly 1 connected port (a terminal). Returns one EXACT
LossPath (the port's open-atmosphere side is None), or UNSUPPORTED
if NeckSize/LossCoefficient aren't set (nothing to compute) or the
port geometry is invalid.

#### `transition_loss(context)`

Loss of a transition: a change of duct size, and possibly of shape,
along a straight axis (SMACNA Tables 14-11 and 14-12).

- Round to round: expansion 14-11 A (by Reynolds number), contraction 14-12 A.
- Rectangular to rectangular: expansion 14-11 E when only one pair of
  sides diverges ("sides straight"), else 14-11 B (pyramidal);
  contraction 14-12 A. The angle is the larger of the two side-pair
  angles (the "major angle" of the tables).
- Round to rectangular, either way: the equivalent angle of 14-11 C/D,
  then 14-11 B for an expansion or 14-12 A for a contraction (the
  latter is not printed for this shape: approximation).
- Oval is read as the rectangle of the same width and height: approximation.

properties["TransitionLength"] is the body length; 0 uses the duct
size (at least 100 mm), as the geometry does. Returns one LossPath
referenced to the outlet's velocity: EXACT when every lookup was
inside a table printed for this fitting, APPROXIMATION (with the
reason) when not, UNSUPPORTED when it cannot be worked out.

#### `uniform_fallback_loss(context, k, warning=None)`

Explicit generic-K policy for a fitting shape with no dedicated
formula (e.g. a true multi-in/multi-out cross): applies `k`
uniformly to every outlet port, same as the old "return a bare
float" convention used to mean -- but now an explicit FALLBACK
result instead of a silently-applied default.

#### `wye_loss(context)`

True Wye (branch.wye) fitting loss: three ports where no pair is a
Tee-style collinear run -- NetworkParser never assigns a
qualifiers["common_leg"] to a Wye, since there's no run/branch
split to name (see TOPOLOGY_CLASSIFICATION.md). This is therefore
a distinct API entry point from branch_loss()/branch_loss_bullhead()
rather than routing a Wye through either of those Tee-oriented
methods -- it never guesses a "straight-through" secondary leg,
since a true Wye has none by definition.

Internally this reuses the same "no independent straight leg"
calculation a bullhead tee/wye needs (see
_no_straight_leg_branch_zetas): each non-common leg is evaluated
independently against the common leg with the diverging/converging
branch-zeta tables. A symmetric wye (equal legs at equal angles
whose areas add up to the common duct's) reads its own tables
instead (see _symmetric_wye_loss); anything else is a reasonable
engineering APPROXIMATION, never presented as an EXACT table value.

Expects exactly 3 connected_ports. Returns one LossPath per leg,
each already referenced to that leg's own velocity, or UNSUPPORTED
for an ambiguous/degenerate flow pattern or invalid geometry.

## Context keys

Each call into library code gets a `context` dict with exactly these keys
(fewer when a key does not apply). `library/contexts.py` is the source.

### Geometry builders and connection lengths

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `hvac_api` | HVACLibraryAPI, the geometry API (see the reference above). |
| `hvac_api_version` | HVACLibraryAPI.API_VERSION. |
| `loss_api` | HVACLossAPI, the loss API. |
| `loss_api_version` | HVACLossAPI.API_VERSION. |
| `construction_layers` | The type-def's construction layers, in order (for build_layered_geometry). |
| `properties` | The type's resolved property values: {name: value}. |
| `type_id` | The type-def id being built. |
| `library_id` | The library id. |
| `family` | The classifier family (e.g. 'branch.tee', 'curved_segment'). |
| `connected_ports` | Junction: the ports, one dict per connected duct, pointing out of the node. |
| `center_point` | Junction: the node position. |
| `analysis` | Junction: the node's topology analysis (collinear pairs, common leg, ...). |
| `topology` | Junction: 'through', 'branch', 'cross', 'multiport' or 'end'. |
| `start_point` | Segment: the trimmed start point. |
| `end_point` | Segment: the trimmed end point. |
| `start_direction` | Segment: the path tangent at the start, pointing along the duct. |
| `end_direction` | Segment: the path tangent at the end, pointing along the duct. |
| `profile` | Segment: 'Circular', 'Rectangular' or 'Oval'. |
| `profile_x_axis` | Segment: the section's x axis (Width direction), or None. |
| `segment_key` | Segment: its stable key in the network. |
| `source_object_name` | Segment: the base sketch or Draft object it was drawn from. |
| `source_index` | Segment: its edge index in that object. |
| `path_kind` | Segment: 'straight' or 'curved'. |
| `path_edge` | Segment: the trimmed path edge of a curved segment, else None. |
| `flange_ports` | Set by a PartScript elbow: its flange ends, for fittings/features.py. |
| `branch_jog` | Set by fittings/taps.with_branch_jog: a side branch moved in to fit the run. |
| `position` | Marker fallback position. |
| `equipment_port` | An end connected to an equipment port: that opening as a port-like dict (profile, section_params, profile_x_axis, position). Absent otherwise. |

### Loss functions

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `hvac_api` | HVACLibraryAPI. |
| `hvac_api_version` | HVACLibraryAPI.API_VERSION. |
| `loss_api` | HVACLossAPI, the loss API. |
| `loss_api_version` | HVACLossAPI.API_VERSION. |
| `construction` | The component's construction (layers and materials). |
| `hydraulic_roughness_mm` | Roughness of the air-side surface, mm. |
| `center_point` | The node position. |
| `properties` | The type's resolved property values. |
| `connected_ports` | The ports, each with flow_rate_lps, velocity_ms and reynolds added by the solver. |
| `family` | The classifier family. |
| `flow_class` | 'diverging', 'converging', 'expansion', ... or '' when unknown. |
| `qualifiers` | Classifier qualifiers, e.g. {'common_leg': 'branch'}. |
| `derived_values` | Values the fitting or classifier derived, e.g. {'area_ratio': 0.5}. |
| `type_id` | The type-def id. |
| `library_id` | The library id. |
| `air_density` | Air density, kg/m3. |
| `air_kinematic_viscosity` | Air kinematic viscosity, m2/s. |
| `equipment_port` | As for geometry: the equipment port an end is connected to, when it is. |

### Friction model factories

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `friction` | The analysis.friction module (DarcyWeisbach, ScaledFriction, ...). |
| `properties` | The segment type's property values. |
| `roughness_mm` | Roughness of the duct surface, mm. |
| `base_model` | The network's own friction model, for a factory to scale or wrap. |
| `type_id` | The segment type-def id. |
| `library_id` | The library id. |
